notes: The single most useful case in this batch. It is the one complaint that both block-quotes the agreement and attaches the whole agreement as an exhibit, so the JobsOhio form Grant Agreement text is public here. Three things stand out. First, the remedy for missing job commitments is a plain repayment demand under Section 9(b)(ii), payable within 30 days, not a clawback formula and not liquidated damages. Second, Section 9 says the listed remedies 'are the sole and exclusive remedies.' Third, Section 5(c) lets JobsOhio waive repayment entirely at its own discretion if the company writes in describing 'Market Conditions and Other Factors,' which Section 5(d) defines broadly enough to include 'an overall decline in economic performance' and 'Grantee's overall presence in the State of Ohio.' Republic Steel is also the only defendant in this batch that hired counsel and answered, and the suit for $300,000 was then dismissed with prejudice four months later with each side bearing its own fees. The $500,000 on the Form 990 schedule does not match the $300,000 pleaded as disbursed under this agreement, and the court record does not reconcile the two.

notes: The timing is the story. JobsOhio sued for the whole $200,000 in September 2021, fifteen months before the Metric Evaluation Date of December 31, 2022, so the job commitments could not yet have been missed. The pleaded breach is entirely documentary: no Annual Reports, and no back-up documentation for an advance JobsOhio had agreed to pay early at the company's request. The company then hired Littler Mendelson, got the default judgment vacated by agreement, and JobsOhio dismissed without prejudice three days later. On JobsOhio's Form 990 schedule the recipient is shown with $0 of cash paid in the matched years, which does not sit easily with the pleaded $200,000 advance; the court record does not reconcile the two and nothing here establishes what, if anything, changed hands. This is the only case in the batch where a default judgment against a JobsOhio defendant was undone.

Grantor has approved an award of financial assistance to Grantee to induce Grantee to undertake and complete the Project with the goal of attracting and retaining business opportunities for the State of Ohio that create and/or retain a significant number of jobs for Ohioans. Accordingly, achieving Grantee's Metric Commitment obligations at the Project site during the Term are essential terms of this Agreement.' That is the only passage of the agreement the pleading block-quotes. It does not quote Section 6(b) or Section 9. || The court's own words on the remedy, from the Decision and Entry of 2021-04-07 granting partial summary judgment, at pages 6 and 7: 'Here, the Court finds that the undisputed facts show that, pursuant to the terms of the Grant Agreement, the MPC bargained for and agreed to accept grant funds conditioned on it creating and maintaining a specified number of jobs and payroll at the Project Site, and making specified fixed asset investments, and maintaining the same from the Metric Evaluation Date of December 31, 2017 through the Metric Expiration Date of December 31, [2]019. After receiving $50,000.00 in grant funds from JobsOhio, MPC sold its assets, ceased its operations, and failed to maintain the Metric Commitments through the Metric Expiration Date of December 31, 2019. Based on the foregoing, MPC is in breach of the Grant Agreement. JobsOhio has demanded repayment of the full grant amount of $50,000.00, and MPC has failed and refused to repay the Grant funds. Significantly, the Grant Agreement provides that JobsOhio may recover the entire grant amount upon a breach. The Grant Agreement is an enforceable contract.' and 'Thus, MPC is contractually and legally obligated to repay the Grant funds to JobsOhio. JobsOhio is, therefore, entitled to summary judgment in its favor and against MPC in the amount of $50,000.00.' The court also stated the governing rule: 'controlling legal precedent holds that a grantee may recover the full amount of its grant funds in the event of a breach if the agreement so specifies,' citing Matrix Centennial, 2014-Ohio-3251.

Not called a clawback and not called liquidated damages. This is the only case in the batch where a judge construed a JobsOhio grant agreement in a written opinion and held the full repayment term enforceable.

notes: The most legally substantial case in the batch. It is the only one that produced a reasoned judicial decision on whether a JobsOhio grant agreement is enforceable and whether the whole grant can be recovered on a breach. Judge Julie M. Lynch held that it can, resting on Matrix Centennial, 2014-Ohio-3251, and rejecting any argument that a grant is a gift rather than a contract. It is also the only case in the batch where JobsOhio pursued the owner personally and the buyer of the business: the amended complaint alleges that Shawn L. Ritchie diverted $600,000 of a $6.5 million purchase price to himself through a consulting agreement and covenant not to compete, took two company vehicles, and caused MPC to pay off a $670,544.02 bank loan that was at least half Montana Jake's obligation, and that MPC 'failed to pay or set aside funds from the sale of its assets to pay current and foreseeable creditors, including JobsOhio.' Those claims were dismissed without prejudice in November 2021 after repeated service failures on Ritchie. The underlying facts are stark: a $50,000 grant reimbursed a $65,526.65 machine, the company created 10 of 30 promised jobs, and then sold the machine and the whole business and closed the site a year before the Metric Expiration Date. Two $50,000 judgments stand on this docket, against the company and against the buyer, and only one is marked satisfied.
